sections.title: Basic Paths and Risks
sections.content:
The 'Settings' tab in the main Manager window is used to configure key directories and application behavior. These are the same paths you configured during the first launch, expanded with advanced features:

  • Projects Root: The main directory where VenvHub Pro looks for your source code (project folders).
  • Venv Hub: The central directory where all virtual environments are physically stored and isolated.
  • Local Packages: The directory for your custom shared modules, which the application dynamically links into venvs without requiring UAC (Linker module).
  • Local Packages (pip -e): The directory for your source packages installed in editable mode (requiring setup.py or pyproject.toml).
  • VS Code Profile: Selection of the active, fully isolated user profile for the Visual Studio Code editor (custom extensions and settings).
Warning Regarding Path Changes!
The application logically links your projects with environments. If you already have existing environments and change the 'Venv Hub' path, the application will look into the new empty folder, find nothing, and your environments will 'disappear' from the table (even though they still physically exist on the old drive).

How to do it properly? If you need to migrate data to another drive (e.g. from C: to D:):
  1. Close VenvHub Pro.
  2. Move the entire Venvs folder to the new drive using Windows Explorer.
  3. Open VenvHub Pro and update the path to the new location in Settings.

sections.title: Package Manager (Pip vs UV)
sections.content:
This is one of the most critical settings defining the application's engine under the hood. It determines which tool is used whenever you click Install, Uninstall, Update, or when environments are created and cloned.

Standard (Pip)

The traditional, time-tested Python standard. It is slower and cannot automatically resolve complex dependency conflicts during bulk updates. Its primary advantage is 100% out-of-the-box compatibility with all systems (no additional tools required).

Ultra-fast (UV - Astral)

An extremely fast tool written in Rust that replaces Pip. Installations are often 10x to 100x faster thanks to global caching. In addition, it unlocks the 'Autopilot' feature, which can automatically repair broken environments after package updates.

UV Availability (Depends on launch method):
  • In the compiled .exe version: The uv binary is already bundled directly inside the application. You do not need to install anything; simply enable it in Settings and it works immediately.
  • When running from Python source code: UV is not part of the standard Python library. VenvHub Pro scans your system with an internal detector. If not found, it displays a notification (prompting you to install it via pip install uv) and safely falls back to Pip, preventing application crashes.

sections.title: Appearance (Themes) and Customization with AI
sections.content:
VenvHub Pro supports full UI customization using .qss (Qt Style Sheets) files, which are the desktop equivalent of web CSS stylesheets.

Dual-Theme System

The application automatically searches and combines themes from two locations:

  1. Built-in: Themes embedded directly in the application source or installation folder (e.g. VS Dark, Dracula, Solarized).
  2. Custom: Themes that you downloaded or created. They are located in the themes folder either next to VenvHubPro.exe (for Portable installation) or in %APPDATA%\VenvHubPro\themes.

Overriding: If your custom directory contains a theme with the exact same name as a built-in theme (e.g., modifying colors in Dracula.qss), the application prioritizes your custom file. You can freely customize official themes without worrying about losing modifications during program updates.

Working with Icons in Themes

Because the application runs as a compiled standalone executable, standard relative image paths in QSS files may not always resolve reliably. Therefore, the system utilizes a combination of dynamic system path replacement and absolute references. To add custom icons, you have the following options:

  • A) Using the built-in themes directory (Recommended for portability):
    The application's internal themes folder serves as default storage. If you copy custom icons here (for example into a subfolder icon/my_icons/ inside the themes folder), you can reference them universally in QSS using the placeholder {{CORE_THEMES_DIR}}.

    Example in .qss:
    qproperty-icon: url({{CORE_THEMES_DIR}}/icon/my_icons/save.svg);
  • B) Using an absolute path:
    If you prefer keeping icons stored in a fixed location outside the application directory, you can use a direct reference (backslashes \ must be converted to forward slashes /).

    Example in .qss:
    qproperty-icon: url(C:/MyIcons/custom_icon.png);

Masterclass: How to Replace Text Emojis with Real SVG Icons

By default, the application uses Emojis or special characters on buttons in many places (▶, 📁, 🔄, ⚙). Through QSS, you can completely replace them with professional SVG icons. However, it is critically important to distinguish between button types:

Scenario 1: Icon-ONLY Buttons (e.g. Play ▶, Folder 📁, Settings ⚙)

Here in QSS, we completely hide the original Emoji character by setting color: transparent !important; and inject your SVG icon:

QPushButton#btn_play {
    color: transparent !important;
    qproperty-icon: url({{CORE_THEMES_DIR}}/icon/play.svg);
    qproperty-iconSize: 16px 16px;
    background-color: transparent;
    border: none;
}

Scenario 2: Buttons with BOTH Icon and Text (e.g. '🔄 Refresh', '❌ Uninstall')

Important note: If you use color: transparent here, the label text will disappear as well. The correct approach is to remove the Emoji directly in the language dictionary files (e.g. translations/en_US.json) and only define qproperty-icon in QSS.
QPushButton#btn_refresh {
    qproperty-icon: url({{CORE_THEMES_DIR}}/icon/refresh.svg);
    qproperty-iconSize: 16px 16px;
    padding-left: 10px;
    text-align: left;
}

Scenario 3: Changing the Window Header Icon (QLabel#lbl_icon)

The icon in the window header is a QLabel; therefore, qproperty-icon does not apply to it. Instead, use qproperty-pixmap combined with forced scaling qproperty-scaledContents: true;:

QLabel#lbl_icon {
    qproperty-scaledContents: true;
    qproperty-pixmap: url({{CORE_THEMES_DIR}}/icon/app_icon.svg);
}
Creating Custom Themes with AI (ChatGPT / Claude): Copy a template such as VS Dark.qss, prompt the AI for color scheme adjustments (e.g. 'Create a Cyberpunk Light theme'), and click Import Theme... in Settings.

sections.title: Language Selection and AI Translations
sections.content:
The application language can be changed at any time in the Quick Settings panel (by clicking ⚙️ on the Mini-Bar).

The dropdown menu contains the Automatic (Auto) option alongside other languages dynamically discovered by scanning the translations/ folder (all .json dictionaries). Switching the language immediately translates the entire user interface.

How to create a new language using AI?
  1. Open the default translation file translations/en_US.json.
  2. Provide it to the AI with the prompt: 'Translate all string values on the right into [Target Language]. Keep all keys on the left unchanged.'
  3. Add the language display name key to the JSON: "_language_name": "German",
  4. Save the file as de_DE.json into the translations/ folder. The new language will appear in the selection menu automatically.
